title: The Servant as a Light to the Nations; Zion Not Forgotten
summary: The Servant speaks to the distant nations: called from the womb, named Israel, and given a mouth like a sword, he confesses that his labor seems wasted, yet he trusts God for his vindication. God answers that restoring Israel is too small a task, and makes him a light for the nations and a covenant for the people, so that captives come home from every direction. Then Zion complains that the LORD has forgotten her, and God replies that a mother may forget her nursing child but he will not forget Zion, whose name is inscribed on his palms, and whose empty streets will overflow with returning children.
story: Chapter 48 ended with the command to leave Babylon. From chapter 49 onward, Cyrus and Babylon are no longer mentioned, and the focus turns to two figures: the Servant of the LORD, who will carry out God's purpose for Israel and the nations, and Zion, the ruined city personified as a grieving mother. The Servant's voice is heard here for the first time in his own words, and his mission goes beyond the political release that Cyrus provided. Cyrus could free captives from Babylon; the Servant will bring Israel back to God and carry God's salvation to the ends of the earth. The second half of the chapter begins a series of passages on Zion's restoration that continues into chapter 54.
historical:
The setting remains the end of the exile and the early years of return. Jerusalem lay in ruins after 587 or 586 BC, its walls broken and its population scattered, which gives force to Zion's complaint in verse 14. The returnees who came back after Cyrus's decree of 539/538 BC found a small, struggling community, and the promise that the land would be “too small” for its people spoke into that emptiness.

Verse 12 names the land of Aswan (Hebrew Sinim), and the Great Isaiah Scroll from Qumran supports the reading Syene, the ancient name of Aswan at Egypt's southern border. Older translations left the word as Sinim, and some once took it to mean China, a view now generally abandoned. A Jewish military colony existed on the nearby island of Elephantine in the Persian period, known from papyri of the fifth century BC, which shows how far Judeans had been scattered.
cultural:
The Servant's weapons in verse 2, a sharp sword and a polished arrow hidden in a quiver, were the tools of a warrior kept ready for the decisive moment, but here they describe his mouth: his power is his word. Being called and named from the womb echoes the call of prophets such as Jeremiah (Jeremiah 1:5) and suggests a life set apart before birth.

The picture of a nursing mother in verse 15 draws on the strongest bond ancient people knew; infants were nursed for two or three years, and a mother's forgetting was nearly unthinkable. Inscribing a name on the palms (verse 16) may reflect the practice of marking the hand with a name as a sign of belonging or remembrance (compare 44:5). Kings caring for Zion's children and queens nursing them (verse 23) reverses the relationship between empire and captive people: the powerful will serve those they once oppressed. The final verses use the harsh language of siege warfare, where starving cities were driven to desperation, to say that Zion's oppressors will destroy themselves.
literary: Verses 1 to 6 are the second of the four Servant Songs identified by Bernhard Duhm, and some scholars extend it to verse 7 or verse 13. Unlike the first song (42:1-4), where God speaks about the Servant, here the Servant speaks in the first person to the nations, reporting his call, his discouragement, and God's answer. The song is followed by an oracle to the Servant (verses 7 to 12), which repeats the language of 42:6 (a covenant for the people) and describes a new exodus, and a hymn calling heaven and earth to rejoice (verse 13). The second half (verses 14 to 26) is a dialogue between Zion and God: Zion's complaint, God's answer with the image of the mother, Zion's astonished questions about where her children came from, and God's final assurance. Questions and answers structure the whole chapter.

outline.t: The second Servant Song: called from the womb, a light for the nations
The despised Servant made a covenant; captives come home
Heaven and earth called to rejoice
Zion's complaint and God's answer: I will not forget you
The nations bring Zion's children home; the tyrant's captives freed

doctrines.note: The Servant is called before birth, named Israel, despised by the nation, and appointed to restore Israel and bring salvation to the ends of the earth. The New Testament sees this pattern fulfilled in Jesus and, in a derived sense, in those who carry his message.

“It is not enough for You to be My Servant, to raise up the tribes of Jacob.” God's purpose for Israel was never merely national restoration. The light is for the nations, and salvation reaches the ends of the earth.
God's faithfulness to Zion is stronger than a mother's love: “Even if she could forget, I will not forget you!” The covenant bond does not break because of exile.
Zion, bereaved and barren, will be astonished by the children who come to her. The chapter pictures hope as more than restoration of what was lost; it is abundance beyond expectation.

words.note: Eved, servant. In verse 3 God says, “You are My Servant, Israel,” yet in verses 5 and 6 the Servant's task is to bring Jacob back and restore Israel. The word thus holds together the Servant's identity with Israel and his mission to Israel, which is the central puzzle of these songs.

Or, light. The Servant is made “a light for the nations.” Light in Isaiah often stands for salvation and revelation breaking into darkness (9:2; 60:1-3). The same phrase appears in 42:6, and it becomes one of the defining descriptions of the Servant's mission.

Shakach, to forget. It appears four times in the dialogue with Zion: Zion says the Lord has forgotten her, and God replies that a mother might forget but he will not. The repetition makes the chapter's answer to the exiles' deepest fear unmistakable.

Riq, empty or in vain. “I have labored in vain.” The Servant's honest discouragement is part of the song. His confidence rests not on visible success but on the conviction that his vindication is with God.

christ: The New Testament draws on this chapter repeatedly. Simeon, holding the infant Jesus in the temple, calls him a light for revelation to the Gentiles and glory to Israel (Luke 2:32), echoing verse 6. Paul and Barnabas quote verse 6 in Acts 13:47 to explain their mission to the Gentiles, applying the Servant's calling to those who carry Christ's message. Paul quotes verse 8 in 2 Corinthians 6:2, declaring that now is the time of favor and the day of salvation. Revelation 7:16-17 echoes verse 10, promising that the redeemed will not hunger or thirst or be struck by the sun, and that the Lamb will guide them to springs of living water. Paul's description of being set apart from his mother's womb (Galatians 1:15) recalls verse 1. The Servant who is Israel yet restores Israel is understood in the New Testament as Jesus, the one faithful Israelite who fulfills Israel's calling and gathers both Israel and the nations to God.

hard.q: The Servant is called Israel in verse 3 but sent to restore Israel in verses 5 and 6. Who is he?
hard.a:
This is the sharpest form of the question raised by all the Servant Songs, and readers have answered it in four main ways. Some identify the Servant with the nation of Israel, or with a faithful remnant within it that is sent to the rest; verse 3 names him Israel, and the word is found in nearly all ancient manuscripts. Others identify the Servant with the prophet himself, who speaks in the first person, reports his call from the womb like Jeremiah, and experiences discouragement in his mission. Others see a particular individual of the prophet's time or a future king. Christians, following the New Testament, identify the Servant ultimately as the Messiah, Jesus.

Many interpreters combine these views. The Servant is called Israel because he embodies what Israel was meant to be; since the nation as a whole has failed its calling (42:18-25; 48:1-8), the role narrows to one who fulfills it and so restores the rest. On this reading, the name Israel is not a contradiction but the key: the Servant is the true Israel sent to Israel and the nations. The New Testament's application of verse 6 both to Jesus (Luke 2:32) and to his messengers (Acts 13:47) shows that it too saw the Servant's work extended through those who belong to him.

questions: The Servant said, “I have labored in vain,” yet trusted God for his reward. How do you keep going when your work seems to bear no fruit?
God says it is not enough to restore Israel; the light is for the nations. What does this say about how wide God's purposes are for his people today?
Zion felt forgotten, and God answered with the image of a mother and her child. When have you felt forgotten by God, and what helped you?
